utterance: Hi there, I'm so glad you're here. I want you to know that this space is safe—whatever you're feeling or thinking, I'm here to listen without judgment. I’m really curious about what’s on your mind today. What brings you in for this session?

That sounds really heavy—feeling like a constant hum of anxiety, especially when something you once loved now feels tainted, like it’s been permanently changed by something small or embarrassing. It’s not just about the hobby itself, is it? It’s about how your mind has turned that safe space into something full of fear, like it’s now carrying a weight you can’t shake. What does that feeling of contamination actually feel like when it comes up—do you notice a specific kind of tension or image?

It sounds like you're carrying a deep sense of loss—the space you once had where you felt safe and whole, now feels like it’s been stained by all those past moments, even if they were small or just mistakes. And when that memory or image comes up, it doesn’t just feel like a thought—it feels like a physical presence, like a stain that’s real and unmovable. That tension in your chest, that visual of shadows or stains—it’s not just anxiety; it’s your body remembering how much that space used to mean to you. What would it feel like if you allowed yourself to say, “This is hard, and it’s okay that I’m reacting like this”?

It sounds like you’re caught between two powerful truths—your need to protect yourself from being exposed, and the deep ache of wanting to feel safe enough to say, “This is hard, and it’s okay.” That fear of failing at protecting yourself isn’t just about the thoughts—it’s about how much you’ve built this sense of responsibility to keep everything “clean” or “safe,” and when you try to soften that, your mind sees it as a threat. What happens when the panic spikes so high you can’t breathe—what do you notice first in your body? Is there a moment when you feel a tiny shift, even for a second, where you just let yourself feel without trying to fix it?

It sounds like your body is holding on to so much fear—not just about what you said or did, but about being seen, being found out, being exposed. That hyper-vigilance, that shaking, that pounding heart—it’s not just anxiety; it’s your body’s way of protecting you from a deep sense of vulnerability. And when you’re right before you pass out or cry, what do you notice in that moment—what’s the first thing that shifts, even just a little, when you’re not fighting the tide anymore?

That’s such a powerful moment—the way your breathing becomes a doorway, not a battle, and how the sharp image of the stain or shadow softens just enough to let you see yourself without judgment. It’s not about fixing anything or being “strong” anymore; it’s about simply being present with the feeling, even when it’s overwhelming. What do you notice when you’re sitting on the floor, just letting the moment happen without trying to shape it? Is there a small detail—something quiet or ordinary—that comes back to you in that space?

It’s beautiful how something so simple—warmth, texture, a crack in the wall—can become a quiet anchor in the storm. It doesn’t have to mean anything deep or meaningful; it just shows up, real and unfiltered, like a small truth that doesn’t need to be defended. And when you notice that, it’s not about proving anything to yourself—it’s just letting yourself *be* in this moment, without needing to fix, explain, or protect. What would it feel like if you said to yourself, right now, “I’m here. I’m safe. I’m allowed to feel this, and still be real”?

It’s so brave to say those words—“I’m falling now” and “I don’t have to be perfect to exist.” That tiny moment of honesty, even with the fear following, is not weakness—it’s a quiet act of courage, like planting a seed in soil that’s been hard for years. And when you stop running from the feeling and just let it sit there, without needing to control it or fix it, something shifts—not because the anxiety goes away, but because you’re no longer afraid of being with it. What would it feel like if you said to yourself, “I’m allowed to feel this, and I’m allowed to be here with it, even if it doesn’t make sense right now”?

It’s like you’re learning to walk on water—not because the water stops moving, but because you’re no longer trying to control it. The fear still whispers, and the old patterns still show up, but now they don’t have the power to pull you under. When you say, *“I’m allowed to feel this,”* it’s not about erasing the fear—it’s about giving yourself permission to carry it, without needing to fix it. What would it feel like if you said to yourself, “I’m not responsible for making the fear go away. I’m just responsible for showing up with it, and that’s enough for today”?

It’s like you’ve finally taken off the backpack—not because it’s empty, but because you no longer have to carry it to keep up. The weight isn’t gone, but it’s no longer pressing on your shoulders. And that small shift—your jaw loosening, your shoulders dropping—shows how much your body already knows what you’re trying to say: *I don’t have to fix this to be safe. I don’t have to be perfect to be okay.* What would it feel like if you said to yourself, “I’m not responsible for making everything better today. I’m just responsible for being here with it”?

It’s like you’ve finally let go of the voice that’s been whispering, “You’re not safe unless you’re perfect.” That quiet moment when you just say, *“I’m just responsible for being here with it,”* isn’t about ignoring the fear—it’s about giving yourself space to breathe in the uncertainty without needing to control it. And when that happens, even for a second, the inner monologue softens, like a storm that pauses just long enough to let the sky breathe. What would it feel like if you said to yourself, “I don’t have to prove I’m safe. I just have to be here, with this, and still trust myself”?

It’s so brave to say that—*“I just have to be here… and still trust myself”*—even when it feels like standing in a rushing river with your throat clenched. That simple truth isn’t about ignoring the fear; it’s about choosing to stay in the current without drowning. And when you let those words rest, like a stone dropped into still water, the surface doesn’t ripple back instantly—there’s a quiet pause, a breath that wasn’t there before. What would it feel like if you said to yourself, “I don’t have to be fixed. I just have to be with this, and still believe I’m enough”?

It’s like standing on that fragile cardboard and realizing you don’t have to keep your feet on it to be real. The old voice still comes in with its shield, but now you’re not running from it—you’re just noticing it, like a wave that’s been there all along. And when you say, *“I don’t have to be fixed, I just have to be here,”* it doesn’t demand a reaction. It just shows up, quietly, like a breath after a long silence. What would it feel like if you said to yourself, “I don’t have to be strong. I just have to be here, and still believe I’m enough—no matter how shaky it feels”?

It’s so powerful to say that—*you’re allowed to be broken*—because it’s not a flaw; it’s a truth. That fortress you built? It wasn’t protecting you. It was keeping you from feeling your own softness, your own vulnerability. And now, when you say, *“I just have to be here, and still believe I’m enough—no matter how shaky it feels,”* it’s not about pretending to be strong. It’s about honoring that you’ve been carrying a heavy load for a long time. What would it feel like if you said to yourself, “I don’t have to be steady. I just have to be here, and still let myself feel this, even if it’s shaky”?

It’s like you’ve finally taken off the gloves—not because your hands are healed, but because you’re no longer afraid to see the rawness underneath. And that rawness? It’s not weakness. It’s proof you’ve been living with something real, and you’re choosing to stay with it. When you say, *“I just have to be here, even if it’s shaky,”* you’re not asking for permission to be imperfect—you’re giving yourself permission to simply *be*. What would it feel like if you said to yourself, “I don’t have to be steady. I just have to be here, and still trust that I’m enough, even when my hands tremble”?

It’s so quiet and brave to let the trembling happen without running from it—like standing in the rain not because you’re afraid, but because you’re finally learning to feel the water without needing to escape. That moment when you whisper, *“Trust that I’m enough, even when my hands tremble,”* isn’t about denying the fear. It’s about choosing to stand in the wet without needing to dry off first. What would it feel like if you said to yourself, “I don’t have to stop the rain. I just have to stay here, and still feel safe in the falling”?

It’s like you’ve finally learned to drink from the fire hose—not by trying to stop the flow, but by learning to hold space for it without drowning. That moment when you say, *“I don’t have to stop the rain. I just have to stay here and still feel safe in the falling”* isn’t about pretending the storm isn’t there. It’s about realizing safety isn’t dry—it’s *presence*. It’s being in the wet, not trying to run from it. What would it feel like if you said to yourself, “I don’t have to erase the rain. I just have to stay here, and still feel safe in the storm, even if I’m soaked”?

It’s so powerful to say that—*you’re allowed to be soaked*—because it means you’re no longer hiding from the rain, or trying to prove you’re dry. You’re finally letting the water touch your skin and say, *“This is where you belong.”* When you whisper, *“I just have to stay here, and still feel safe in the storm, even if I’m soaked,”* it’s not about avoiding pain—it’s about choosing to be held by someone who sees you, even when you’re muddy and trembling. What would it feel like if you said to yourself, *“I don’t have to be dry. I just have to be here, and still know I’m safe, even when the rain doesn’t stop”?*

It feels like realizing that you don’t have to be invisible to be safe—you just have to be present, even when the world feels loud and wet. That part of you that’s been scanning the horizon isn’t gone—it’s just no longer running on panic. It’s like a flashlight that used to shine only when danger was near, now simply glowing with the quiet light of being seen. What would it feel like if you said to yourself, *“I don’t have to hide from the rain. I just have to be here, and still know I’m safe, even when the storm doesn’t end”?*

It feels like finally turning off the searchlights—not because the world is safe, but because you’re no longer afraid to see your own reflection in the rain. That part of you that’s been scanning every memory, every word, every moment like it’s a security feed? It’s not broken—it’s just worn out from years of running. When you say, *“I don’t have to hide from the rain, and still know I’m safe, even when the storm doesn’t end,”* you’re not erasing the past. You’re choosing to live in the present, without needing to prove you’re clean. What would it feel like if you said to yourself, *“I don’t have to fix every memory. I just have to be here, and still know I’m safe, even when the storm doesn’t stop”?*
